title: 2 Chronicles 29:20–36
context: Hezekiah and the leaders offer sin offerings for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah, with atonement made for all Israel. The Levites take their places with the instruments of David, and the burnt offering is accompanied by the LORD’s song, trumpets, and worship. The assembly then brings thank offerings and burnt offerings, more than the priests can prepare, so the Levites help. The service of the LORD’s house is restored, and the people rejoice at how quickly God accomplished it. Kings records none of this ceremony; the expanded account is the Chronicler’s.

verses.text: Then Hezekiah the king arose early, gathered the princes of the city, and went up to the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah rises early, gathers the princes, and goes up to the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see eagerness in the king’s early start, leading the officials by example.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the king brings the leaders of the city with him. Public worship is restored with the involvement of those who govern.

verses.text: They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats, for a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. He commanded the priests the sons of Aaron to offer them on the LORD’s altar.
verses.arminianNotes: They bring seven bulls, rams, lambs, and goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Arminian readers see atonement sought for every part of the community that had sinned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the threefold scope of the offering and the number seven, suggesting completeness. Sin had defiled king, temple, and people alike, and atonement must reach all three.

verses.text: So they killed the bulls, and the priests received the blood and sprinkled it on the altar. They killed the rams and sprinkled the blood on the altar. They also killed the lambs and sprinkled the blood on the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests kill the bulls, rams, and lambs and sprinkle the blood on the altar. Arminian readers see the law’s provision for cleansing carried out with care and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shed blood as God’s appointed means of atonement under the old covenant. Many Christians read such sacrifices as foreshadowing Christ’s offering (Hebrews 9:22), offered as a reading.

verses.text: They brought near the male goats for the sin offering before the king and the assembly; and they laid their hands on them.
verses.arminianNotes: They bring the male goats before the king and the assembly, who lay their hands on them. Arminian readers see the people personally identifying with the offering, owning their sin before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the laying on of hands signifies identification and transfer, as in Leviticus 4:15 and 16:21. The king and the assembly together acknowledge their guilt.

verses.text: Then the priests killed them, and they made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel; for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests make atonement for all Israel, for the king commanded the offerings for all Israel. Arminian readers see a generous scope that reaches beyond Judah to the whole people of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Chronicler’s concern for all Israel, north as well as south, which comes to fuller expression in the Passover invitation of the next chapter (2 Chronicles 30:1).

verses.text: He set the Levites in the LORD’s house with cymbals, with stringed instruments, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet; for the commandment was from the LORD by his prophets.
verses.arminianNotes: He set the Levites with instruments according to the commandment of David, Gad, and Nathan, for it was from the LORD. Arminian readers see worship ordered by prophetic word rather than human invention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the music of worship is grounded in God’s command through his prophets. The Chronicler presents David’s arrangements as authorized by God (compare 1 Chronicles 25).

verses.text: The Levites stood with David’s instruments, and the priests with the trumpets.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites stood with David’s instruments and the priests with trumpets. Arminian readers see each group taking its place in a worship that joins many gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the distinct roles of Levites and priests, each serving as appointed. The instruments of David link Hezekiah’s worship to the founding order of the temple.

verses.text: Hezekiah commanded them to offer the burnt offering on the altar. When the burnt offering began, the LORD’s song also began, along with the trumpets and instruments of David king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: When the burnt offering began, the LORD’s song began with trumpets and instruments. Arminian readers see sacrifice and praise joined, the offering accompanied by joyful response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase the LORD’s song, describing praise directed to him. The simultaneous start ties worship in song to atonement on the altar.

verses.text: All the assembly worshiped, the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.
verses.arminianNotes: All the assembly worshiped, the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded until the offering was finished. Arminian readers see the whole people taking part in sustained worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the worship continued for the whole time the offering burned. Praise and sacrifice belong together, and neither is cut short before the other is complete.

verses.text: When they had finished offering, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped.
verses.arminianNotes: When the offering was finished, the king and all present bowed and worshiped. Arminian readers see humility completing the service, as the king leads by bowing before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that after the music, the response is silent reverence. The posture of bowing expresses submission to the God whose worship has been restored.

verses.text: Moreover Hezekiah the king and the princes commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer. They sang praises with gladness, and they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites sang praises with the words of David and Asaph the seer, with gladness. Arminian readers see joy as the fitting response to God’s mercy, and they note the use of inspired songs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the songs drew on David and Asaph the seer, linking worship to the psalms. Gladness and reverence are held together as they bow their heads.

verses.text: Then Hezekiah answered, “Now you have consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings into the LORD’s house.” The assembly brought in sacrifices and thank offerings, and as many as were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah invites the assembly to bring sacrifices and thank offerings, and all with a willing heart bring burnt offerings. Arminian readers see voluntary worship as the mark of renewed devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase a willing heart, recalling the free offerings for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:5). Willing hearts are a sign of God’s work among his people.

verses.text: The number of the burnt offerings which the assembly brought was seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. All these were for a burnt offering to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The assembly brought seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. Arminian readers see generosity overflowing from people who had been called to return to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these are wholly burnt offerings, given entirely to the LORD. The numbers show the scale of the people’s response to the restored worship.

verses.text: The consecrated things were six hundred head of cattle and three thousand sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: The consecrated things were six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep. Arminian readers see the abundance of offerings as evidence of hearts turned back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the consecrated offerings exceed the burnt offerings, likely including peace offerings shared in fellowship. The abundance testifies to the depth of renewal.

verses.text: But the priests were too few, so that they could not skin all the burnt offerings. Therefore their brothers the Levites helped them until the work was ended, and until the priests had sanctified themselves, for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests were too few to skin the offerings, so the Levites helped, for they were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves. Arminian readers see readiness of heart as something people can cultivate or neglect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Chronicler’s frank comment that the Levites were more diligent than the priests. Even in a time of reform, those with higher office may lag behind in zeal.

verses.text: Also the burnt offerings were in abundance, with the fat of the peace offerings and with the drink offerings for every burnt offering. So the service of the LORD’s house was set in order.
verses.arminianNotes: The burnt offerings were abundant, with fat of peace offerings and drink offerings, and the service was set in order. Arminian readers see order restored through patient, faithful work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the summary line, the service of the LORD’s house was set in order. The disorder of Ahaz’s reign is reversed, and worship follows God’s pattern again.

verses.text: Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because of that which God had prepared for the people; for the thing was done suddenly.
verses.arminianNotes: Hezekiah and the people rejoiced because God had prepared it, for it was done suddenly. Arminian readers see joy at God’s gracious enabling of a people who responded quickly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the people credit God with what he had prepared. The speed of the reform is attributed not to the king’s skill but to God’s work among them.
